justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an asset trading near the 255–256 range. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, assuming mean-reversion tendencies dominate over very short windows and that no major catalysts were imminent. The slight upward drift in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a gentle positive trend assumption — essentially that the underlying momentum or fundamental backdrop is marginally constructive, but not dramatically so. The incremental increases are small because I did not want to extrapolate aggressively without strong directional signals.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each time horizon. For the one-day window, daily price fluctuations in a normal market environment tend to be relatively contained, so a range of roughly plus or minus six points felt reasonable. At one week, I widened the interval to reflect the compounding uncertainty of multiple trading sessions, news flow, and intraday volatility. By one month, the interval expands significantly — to a roughly 48-point range — because a full month introduces macroeconomic data releases, potential policy shifts, earnings or sector news, and shifts in market sentiment that are genuinely difficult to anticipate. The widths grow roughly in proportion to the square root of time, consistent with standard diffusion-based thinking about price uncertainty.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected macroeconomic shock — such as a sharp deterioration in employment data, an abrupt central bank policy shift toward tightening, or a geopolitical escalation — could drive prices well below the lower bound of my one-month range. Liquidity events or sudden risk-off sentiment can produce moves that dwarf normal volatility assumptions. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — better-than-expected economic data, a dovish policy pivot, or sector-specific tailwinds — could push prices above the upper bound. My intervals implicitly assume roughly normal market conditions, so fat-tail events, which occur more frequently than standard models suggest, remain a genuine source of extrainterval risk at all three horizons.
